title: Verb Patterns
tagline: Transitive, intransitive and linking verbs, two objects, *-ing* or *to*-infinitive, verb + object + verb, causatives, phrasal verbs, verbs with prepositions, the passive, and reflexive and reciprocal verbs
summary: Each English verb comes with its own patterns: what can follow it, and in which form. This course covers transitive, intransitive and linking verbs, verbs with two objects, the choice between *-ing* and the *to*-infinitive, verbs followed by an object and another verb, causatives such as *make* and *let*, phrasal and prepositional verbs, the passive voice, and reflexive and reciprocal verbs.

chapters.title: Transitive, intransitive and linking verbs
chapters.summary: Verbs that need an object, verbs that cannot take one, verbs that can do both, and linking verbs such as *be*, *seem* and *become*.

chapters.title: Verbs with two objects
chapters.summary: *Give her the book* and *give the book to her*, which verbs allow both patterns, and which take *to* and which *for*.

chapters.title: *-ing* or *to*-infinitive
chapters.summary: Verbs followed by *-ing* (*enjoy*, *avoid*), by *to* (*want*, *decide*), or by either with a change of meaning (*remember*, *stop*, *try*).

chapters.title: Verb + object + verb
chapters.summary: *Want someone to do*, *see someone do* or *doing*, and *help someone (to) do*: the patterns with an object before a second verb.

chapters.title: *Make*, *let*, *have* and *get*
chapters.summary: Causative verbs for making, allowing and arranging things, and *have something done*.

chapters.title: Phrasal verbs
chapters.summary: Verbs with particles such as *give up*, *look after* and *take off*, where the object goes, and how particles like *up* and *out* add meaning.

chapters.title: Verbs with prepositions
chapters.summary: *Depend on*, *consist of*, *apologise for* and other verb–preposition pairs, and the prepositions that follow common adjectives and nouns.

chapters.title: The passive
chapters.summary: How the passive is formed in each tense, when English prefers it, the *get*-passive, and why English uses the passive more often, and more neutrally, than Chinese uses 被.

chapters.title: Reflexive and reciprocal verbs
chapters.summary: *Myself* and *yourself*, *each other* and *one another*, and verbs such as *relax*, *concentrate* and *meet* that usually need neither.
